sections.h: Who qualifies for a VA loan?
p: Veterans, active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, and some surviving spouses can qualify. You prove eligibility with a Certificate of Eligibility (COE), which we can usually pull online in minutes.
At least 90 continuous days if you're on active duty now; for most veterans who served after 1990, 24 continuous months or the full period you were called to (at least 90 days)
6 creditable years in the National Guard or Selected Reserve, or 90 days of active duty, including 30 consecutive days for Guard members
Surviving spouses of service members who died in service or from a service-connected disability

sections.h: What is the VA funding fee?
p: The VA funding fee is a one-time charge that keeps the program running. It can be rolled into your loan, and it is waived entirely if you receive VA disability compensation.
Purchase-loan rates. Purple Heart recipients on active duty and eligible surviving spouses are also exempt.

sections.h: Is there a VA loan limit?
p: No, not if you have full entitlement. Since 2020, borrowers with full entitlement can buy a home of any price with no down payment, as long as they qualify for the payment.
If part of your entitlement is tied up in another VA loan, county loan limits still apply to how much you can borrow with $0 down. Brian will calculate your remaining entitlement for you.

sections.h: Can I use my VA loan more than once?
p: Yes. VA benefits can be used again and again. You can restore your entitlement when you sell, and in some cases you can have two VA loans at the same time, such as after a PCS move.
That flexibility matters for families stationed at NAS Pensacola, NAS Whiting Field, Coast Guard Sector Mobile, Maxwell AFB, or Redstone Arsenal who want to keep their first home as a rental.

sections.h: What is a home equity loan?
p: A home equity loan is a second mortgage that pays you a lump sum at closing, secured by your home. You repay it with a fixed rate and the same monthly payment for the whole term, while your first mortgage stays in place.
Terms usually run 10 to 30 years. Because the rate and payment never change, it is easy to budget for, and you pay interest on the full amount from the start.

sections.h: How much can I borrow with a home equity loan?
p: Lenders limit how much your mortgage plus your home equity loan can total compared with your home's value, and that limit varies by lender. For example, if a lender allows 85% on a $400,000 home with a $210,000 balance, that is a loan of up to about $130,000.
Your credit score, income, and the property type set where you land in that range. The calculator below runs the numbers for your home.

sections.h: Home equity loan or cash-out refinance?
p: If your current mortgage rate is lower than today's rates, a home equity loan usually wins because you keep that rate and borrow only the extra. A cash-out refinance makes more sense when you can also lower the rate on your first mortgage.
Brian will compare both, including closing costs and the blended rate, before you decide.

sections.h: What can I use a home equity loan for?

sections.h: Home equity loan or HELOC: what's the difference?
p: A home equity loan pays you one lump sum at closing with a fixed rate and a fixed monthly payment. A HELOC (home equity line of credit) is a revolving line you draw from as needed, usually with a variable rate and interest-only payments at first.

A home equity loan fits when you know the amount you need, such as a roof quote or a debt payoff figure, and want a payment that never changes. A HELOC fits ongoing costs you can't price yet, if you're comfortable with a rate that can rise. Brian offers both and can compare them for your home.

Walk through a specific home with the Gulf Coast home cost checklist, or enter each figure in the payment calculator, which has separate wind and flood fields.

sections.h: What can keep a Gulf Shores condo from qualifying for financing?
p: Usually the building, not the buyer. For a conventional or VA loan, the condo project itself must qualify, and beachfront towers most often fall short because they run like a hotel, are in litigation, need critical repairs, set aside too little for reserves, or have one owner holding too many units.
Hotel-style operations: a rental desk, daily housekeeping, mandatory rental pools, or rules that limit when owners can use their units. Fannie Mae Selling Guide B4-2.1-03, Ineligible Projects
Litigation: pending or threatened lawsuits involving the association, such as construction-defect claims. B4-2.1-03
Critical repairs: significant deferred maintenance or structural work the building still needs. B4-2.1-03

Thin reserves: in a full project review, Fannie Mae looks for at least 10% of the association’s budget going to replacement reserves, or an acceptable reserve study. Fannie Mae Selling Guide B4-2.2-01, Full Review Process
Single-entity ownership: one person or company owning too large a share of the units. B4-2.1-03
VA loans: the condo project must be on VA’s approved list. VA condo report

A building that doesn’t qualify usually needs a non-warrantable condo loan, which typically means a larger down payment and a higher rate. Brian checks the project before you make an offer, so you aren’t surprised after you’re under contract. Ask Brian to check a building.

sections.h: Do I need flood insurance on the Gulf Coast?
p: If the home is in a FEMA high-risk flood zone (zones beginning with A or V) and you use a federally backed mortgage, flood insurance is required. Outside those zones it's optional, but it is often worth pricing near the water.
Look up any address on FEMA’s Flood Map Service Center before you make an offer, and get a flood quote early, because it can change your monthly payment more than the interest rate does.

sections.h: How does wind and hurricane insurance affect my mortgage payment?
p: Near the coast, wind and hail coverage can be one of the largest parts of your housing cost, and in some areas it is excluded from a standard homeowners policy and bought separately. Lenders require the home to be insured for wind, so price it before you commit.
Brian builds your payment estimate with real insurance figures, not a placeholder, so the number you plan around is the number you'll pay.

sections.h: What is a FORTIFIED roof, and does it lower insurance?
p: FORTIFIED is a construction standard from the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety for roofs and homes built to resist high winds. Alabama law requires insurers to offer discounts on the wind portion of a policy for homes with a FORTIFIED designation, which can lower your monthly payment.
When you’re comparing homes, ask whether the roof has a FORTIFIED certificate. Learn about FORTIFIED · Does a FORTIFIED roof lower my mortgage payment?

sections.h: What taxes are due at closing in Alabama and Florida?
p: Alabama charges a mortgage recording tax of 15 cents per $100 of the loan amount. Florida charges documentary stamp tax on the note of 35 cents per $100 plus an intangible tax of 0.2% of the loan amount. On a $300,000 loan, that's about $450 in Alabama and about $1,650 in Florida.
Which fits? For the same loan, Florida's mortgage taxes run higher than Alabama's, so budget more cash to close in Florida. Your Loan Estimate lists each tax in Section E.

sections.h: Who can help me get a mortgage when I move from the Midwest to the Gulf Coast?
p: Brian Lehmann (NMLS #369470) of Weber Mortgage, a loan officer since 2010, lends anywhere in Alabama and Florida and works with buyers relocating to Baldwin County, Mobile, Pensacola, and the Florida Panhandle. He is also a licensed home inspector and insurance agent, so he can explain the costs that work differently here before you make an offer.

Buyers from Illinois, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, and Minnesota usually know mortgages well. What surprises them is everything around the loan: wind and flood insurance, homes without basements, property taxes that reset after a sale in Florida, and hurricane season timing. This page covers those differences in plain language.

sections.h: What do Midwest buyers look for when they move to the Gulf Coast?
p: Most want warmer winters, lower property taxes, and an easier lifestyle near the water, without giving up good schools, healthcare, and a reasonable drive to an airport. On the ground that usually means single-level homes, newer construction, a big garage, and a short drive to the beach, the bay, or a golf course.
No more snow and ice. Mild winters are the number one reason people give for moving south.

Lower ongoing costs. Alabama’s property taxes are among the lowest in the country, and Florida has no state income tax. Insurance runs higher than up north, so the full monthly payment is what matters.
Single-story living. Retirees and near-retirees often want everything on one floor.
Newer construction. New subdivisions in Foley, Gulf Shores, Fairhope, Daphne, Spanish Fort, Loxley, Pace, and Navarre offer newer roofs, which usually cost less to insure.
Room for toys. Without basements, buyers look for two- and three-car garages and space for a boat, golf cart, or RV.
Water and golf. Boating, fishing, the beaches, and golf communities are a big draw.
Schools and healthcare. Families ask about Baldwin County and Santa Rosa County schools; retirees ask about hospitals and specialists in Fairhope, Foley, Mobile, and Pensacola.
Getting back home. Easy I-10 access and flights from Pensacola International and Mobile matter when family is still in the Midwest.

sections.h: Are property taxes lower on the Gulf Coast than in the Midwest?
p: In Alabama, usually by a wide margin. Alabama’s average effective property tax rate is under half a percent, among the lowest in the nation, while Illinois’s is around 2%, among the highest. Florida’s rates sit in between and depend on the county and on whether you claim a homestead exemption.

Alabama: a home you live in is taxed at a lower assessment class once you file for the homestead exemption with the county revenue commissioner. A second home or rental doesn’t qualify, so its tax bill can be roughly double the same home’s owner-occupied bill.

Florida: a primary residence can get a homestead exemption of up to $50,000, and the Save Our Homes rule caps yearly increases in its assessed value at 3% or the change in inflation, whichever is lower. You must own and live in the home on January 1 and apply with the county property appraiser by March 1. Starting in 2027, Amendment 3 raises the exemption from non-school taxes to $150,000, then $250,000 in 2028. If you aren’t a Florida resident on December 31, 2026, you get the existing exemption at first and the larger one starting with your fifth year of exemption, so plan your first years of taxes on the current amount. Read the Amendment 3 guide.

The Florida surprise: the seller’s homestead benefits don’t transfer to you. After a sale the assessed value resets toward market value, so your first full tax bill can be much higher than the seller’s. Brian estimates your taxes from the price you pay, not the listing’s last bill.
Tax rules change, and your situation is your own; check details with the county or a tax professional.

sections.h: Why don't homes on the Gulf Coast have basements?
p: The land is low and flat with a high water table and sandy soil, so a basement would sit in groundwater. Most homes here are built on a concrete slab, and homes near the water are often raised on pilings or a stem wall to stay above flood levels.

Plan where your storage and mechanicals will go: the water heater and HVAC are usually in the garage, a closet, or the attic, and the garage does the job a basement did up north. Near the water, the home’s elevation compared with the flood map can change flood insurance a lot, so ask whether the seller has an elevation certificate.

sections.h: How is homeowners insurance different on the Gulf Coast than in the Midwest?
p: The big risk here is wind and water from tropical storms, not hail and frozen pipes. Expect a separate hurricane or named-storm deductible, often a percentage of the home’s insured value, and near the beaches wind may be covered by a separate policy. Flood insurance is always a separate policy.
Roof age matters more. Many insurers price heavily on the roof’s age and condition, and some won’t write an older roof at all.

FORTIFIED roofs and wind mitigation. Alabama requires insurers to offer wind discounts for FORTIFIED homes, and the Strengthen Alabama Homes program has offered grants of up to $10,000 toward a FORTIFIED roof (check current rules and dates). In Florida, a wind mitigation inspection can document features that earn premium credits.
Flood. Required for a federally backed loan in high-risk zones (A and V), and worth pricing in zone X too.
At closing. Lenders usually collect the first year’s premium plus a few months for escrow, so higher premiums also raise your cash to close.
See how this plays out in the Gulf Coast home cost checklist, which walks through two homes at the same price. You’re free to choose any insurance agent.

sections.h: Can I buy on the Gulf Coast before I sell my house up north?
p: Often, yes. If your income and debts allow it, you can qualify while still carrying your current mortgage. Many buyers also take out a home equity loan on their Midwest home for the down payment, then pay it off when that home sells.
Carry both payments: the lender counts your current house payment in your debt-to-income ratio until it’s sold.
Tap equity first: take out a home equity loan on your current home before you list it, while you still live there.
Keep it as a rental: with a signed lease, part of the expected rent may be counted toward qualifying, depending on the loan program.
Buy contingent on your sale: possible, but a sale contingency makes your offer weaker in a competitive neighborhood.
Brian can compare these side by side with your real numbers before you list your current home. Read the full answer on buying before you sell.

sections.h: Should I buy a second home now and retire to the Gulf Coast later?
p: That's a common plan. A second home you’ll use yourself is financed differently from a rental and can be converted to your primary residence when you move. Tell your lender exactly how you plan to use the home; occupancy affects the loan, the rate, and the property taxes.
If you’ll rent it out short term while you’re still working, look at an investor or DSCR loan instead. Homestead exemptions in both states apply only once the home is your primary residence.

sections.h: Should I buy in Alabama or Florida?
p: It depends on your income, your budget, and the town you want. Florida has no state income tax and homestead protections; Alabama has lower property taxes, lower closing taxes, and doesn’t tax Social Security or most traditional pensions. Many buyers look at both sides of the Perdido River before deciding.

Closing taxes differ too: Alabama’s mortgage tax is 15 cents per $100 of the loan, while Florida charges 35 cents per $100 in documentary stamp tax plus a 0.2% intangible tax. On a $300,000 loan that’s about $450 in Alabama and about $1,650 in Florida. A tax professional can tell you what the income tax difference means for you.

p: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac · UAD 3.6 and the new URAR

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac now require a redesigned appraisal report. Here’s what changed, what the appraiser will look at, and how buyers, sellers, and agents can keep the appraisal from slowing down a closing in Alabama and Florida.
Written and reviewed by Brian Lehmann, NMLS #369470, loan officer since 2010 and licensed home inspector · Updated November 19, 2026 · 13-minute read
Since November 2, 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac require the redesigned appraisal report (the new URAR, built on UAD 3.6) for most conventional loans.
Appraisers now photograph every kitchen, bathroom, and bedroom, include a labeled floor plan, measure to the ANSI standard, and rate interior and exterior condition separately.
Agents can avoid delays by preparing the home and the paperwork before the appraiser arrives.

Since November 2, 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac require a new appraisal report for most conventional loans: the redesigned Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR), built on UAD 3.6. One report replaces the old forms and adds more interior photos (every kitchen, bathroom, and bedroom), a labeled floor plan, ANSI square footage, separate interior and exterior condition ratings, and defects tied to where they are. For buyers it means a more detailed report and possibly a little more time; for real estate agents it means preparing the home and the paperwork before the appraiser arrives.

sections.h: What is the new appraisal system Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac require?
p: It is a redesigned appraisal report called the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR), built on a new data standard called the Uniform Appraisal Dataset 3.6 (UAD 3.6). One dynamic report replaces the separate legacy forms, such as Form 1004 for single-family homes, Form 1073 for condos, Form 1025 for two- to four-unit homes, and Form 2055 for exterior-only appraisals.

The old forms dated from 2005, and the data standard behind them from 2011. The new report changes with the property and the assignment, so a condo appraisal shows condo sections and a home with an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) shows ADU sections. Most of the free-text comments and abbreviation codes are gone, replaced by standard answer choices that lenders, underwriters, and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can read the same way. Photos now sit next to the part of the report they support instead of at the back.
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac designed it together, and it is used for loans sold to either one. That covers most conventional mortgages.

sections.h: When did the new appraisal report become mandatory?
p: November 2, 2026. Appraisal reports first submitted to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac on or after that date must use UAD 3.6 and the new URAR. A small number of lenders were granted a temporary exception to keep using the old format until May 19, 2027, and the old format is retired completely on June 28, 2027.

If your home loan appraisal is ordered now, expect it on the new report. Appraisals finished on the old forms before the mandate may still be used on loans in process, and lenders can resubmit them; ask your loan officer how your file is handled.

sections.h: What does the new appraisal mean for homebuyers?
p: Expect a longer, more detailed report with more photos, a floor plan of the home, separate interior and exterior condition ratings, and a clear list of any defects the appraiser found. It does not change how much you can borrow or what an appraisal is for: the lender still needs an independent opinion of the home’s market value.

More photos inside. At a minimum, the appraiser photographs every kitchen, every bathroom, the main living areas including all bedrooms, any finished or unfinished below-grade space, any defect or damage, and examples of recent updates.

A floor plan. The report includes a floor plan or footprint sketch with exterior dimensions to the nearest tenth of a foot and labeled rooms, plus a separate sketch for each additional structure such as an ADU.

An appraisal is not a home inspection. It looks at value and at whether the home meets the loan’s property requirements, not at everything a buyer should know. You still want your own inspection, and you’re free to choose any inspector.

sections.h: What does the new appraisal mean for real estate agents?
p: More of the house is documented, so preparation matters more. Every bedroom and bathroom is photographed, the square footage is measured to the ANSI standard, visible defects are called out by location, and features like a FORTIFIED roof or impact windows can be reported as data. Agents who prepare the home and the paperwork before the appraiser arrives help keep the appraisal, and the closing date, on track.

Listing agents: make sure the appraiser can reach and photograph every room, outbuilding, and ADU, and that utilities are on. Fix small visible defects early, and have a list of updates with dates ready.
Buyer agents: build realistic time into the appraisal contingency, and explain to buyers why the appraisal’s square footage or condition ratings may read differently from the listing.
Both: share facts, such as recent sales and the property’s updates, through the lender’s process. Appraiser independence rules still apply: no one may pressure an appraiser toward a value.

sections.h: Why might the appraisal's square footage differ from the listing?
p: Because Fannie Mae requires appraisers to measure to the ANSI standard (ANSI Z765), and listings often aren’t measured that way. Under ANSI, space with a low ceiling, space reached only through an unfinished area, and below-grade space are reported separately from finished above-grade living area, so the appraisal’s total can be smaller than the number on the listing.

Common examples are a bonus room over the garage with sloped ceilings, a finished space you can only reach through the garage, or square footage copied from tax records. The appraiser must explain why any area doesn’t meet the standard. If you list a home, consider having it measured to ANSI so buyers aren’t surprised.

sections.h: What counts as a defect, damage, or deficiency on the new appraisal?
p: Anything significant that measurably affects the home’s value or marketability, or that must be completed before the loan can close. The appraiser reports it in the section of the report where it belongs, such as the roof, a bathroom, or the foundation, and the lender may require it to be fixed before closing.

Typical examples include roof damage or active leaks, water intrusion, missing handrails on stairs, inoperable systems, broken windows, exposed wiring, and unfinished construction. Cosmetic wear usually isn’t a defect, but it can still show up in the condition ratings.

sections.h: How does the new appraisal report treat hurricane and energy features on the Gulf Coast?
p: The new dataset has places to record disaster mitigation features and energy efficiency features, so items like a FORTIFIED roof, impact-rated windows or storm shutters, and solar panels can be reported as structured data instead of a passing comment. Whether a feature changes the value depends on what local sales show.

On the Alabama coast and in Northwest Florida, have the proof ready: a FORTIFIED certificate, a wind mitigation inspection report, an elevation certificate for homes near the water, and permits or invoices for a new roof or windows. sections.h: What are the loan limits in Baldwin County, Alabama?

sections.h: How much are property taxes in Baldwin County?
p: Alabama taxes a home you live in on 10% of its appraised value, then multiplies that by the local millage. Inside Gulf Shores city limits the 2025 millage is 33 mills, so a home appraised at $400,000 owes about $1,320 a year before the homestead exemption.
Millage depends on the exact tax district, including the school district, so check the parcel with the Baldwin County Revenue Commission. Compare these with Escambia County in the property tax guide.

sections.h: Do second homes and rentals pay more property tax in Alabama?
p: Rentals do. A rental is income-producing property, Class II, assessed at 20% of its appraised value instead of 10%, so the tax roughly doubles. In Gulf Shores that is about $2,640 a year on a home appraised at $400,000, compared with about $1,320 at 10%. A second home you don’t rent out can be Class III, assessed at 10% like a home you live in, but it doesn’t get the homestead exemption.

That difference matters when you compare a beach condo you plan to rent with one you plan only to use yourself. If you plan to rent a second home even part of the year, ask the Baldwin County Revenue Commission which class applies. Brian uses the right class when he estimates your payment.

sections.h: How does the Alabama homestead exemption work?
p: If the home is your primary residence, file for the homestead exemption with the Baldwin County Revenue Commission. The standard exemption (H-1) removes $4,000 of assessed value from state taxes and $2,000 from county taxes.
Owners 65 and older and owners with disabilities can qualify for larger exemptions. The Alabama Department of Revenue lists each one and its income limits.

sections.h: What does it cost to record a mortgage in Baldwin County?
p: Alabama charges a mortgage recording tax of 15 cents per $100 of the loan amount, paid at closing. On a $300,000 loan that is about $450.

sections.h: How do Baldwin County and Escambia County property taxes compare?

sections.h: How is Alabama property tax calculated?

In Gulf Shores, at 33 mills, a $400,000 home you live in owes about $1,320 a year.

sections.h: Do you really need 20% down to buy a house?
p: No. Most loan programs let you buy with much less: 3.5% down with FHA, as little as 3% to 5% with a conventional loan, and 0% with a VA or USDA loan for borrowers who qualify. Twenty percent down removes private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan and lowers the payment, but it’s a choice, not a requirement.

The bigger question is what each option costs. The down payment changes how much cash you need to close far more than it changes the monthly payment, because a smaller down payment comes with mortgage insurance or a program fee. The worksheet below shows both for the same home.

sections.h: What does 20% down actually buy you?
p: A smaller loan and no PMI, so a lower monthly payment. The trade is more cash up front: on a $350,000 home, going from 5% down to 20% down takes another $52,500 at closing.

Divide that extra cash by the monthly savings to see how long the lower payment takes to pay you back. The worksheet does this for you. With the sample figures, it takes several years. Conventional PMI doesn’t last forever, either: you can ask to cancel it once you reach 20% equity based on the original value, and it ends automatically at 22% equity under the original payment schedule, so the gap shrinks over time.
FHA works differently. With less than 10% down, the yearly FHA premium generally lasts for the life of the loan unless you refinance. See FHA loans for the details.

A refinance usually makes sense when what you save each month pays back the closing costs before you expect to sell or refinance again, or when you need to change the loan itself, such as taking cash out, dropping mortgage insurance, or moving to a shorter term.

To find your break-even point, divide the closing costs by the monthly savings. For example, $6,000 in closing costs and a payment that drops by $150 a month break even after 40 months, a little over three years. sections.h: What kinds of refinance are there?
p: There are three main kinds. A rate-and-term refinance changes your rate, term, or loan type with little or no cash back. A cash-out refinance replaces your loan with a larger one and pays you the difference. A streamline refinance lowers the rate on an existing FHA or VA loan with less paperwork.

Which fits? Rate-and-term fits when the goal is a lower rate, a shorter term, or switching from FHA to conventional. Cash-out fits when you need a lump sum and the new rate still works for you. If you already have an FHA or VA loan, look at the streamline first, since it usually costs less and moves faster.

sections.h: Cash-out refinance, home equity loan, or HELOC?
p: A cash-out refinance replaces your first mortgage with a larger one. A home equity loan and a home equity line of credit (HELOC) are second mortgages that leave your first mortgage and its rate in place. A home equity loan pays a lump sum at a fixed rate; a HELOC lets you draw as needed, usually at a variable rate.

Which fits? It depends on how your current rate compares with today's rates. If your current rate is lower, a home equity loan or HELOC keeps it, and only the new money is borrowed at today's rate. If your current rate is higher, or you want a single payment, a cash-out refinance can make more sense. Brian offers cash-out refinances, fixed-rate home equity loans, and HELOCs, and can compare them with your numbers.

sections.h: Can a refinance remove mortgage insurance?
p: Yes. Refinancing an FHA loan into a conventional loan with at least 20% equity removes FHA mortgage insurance, which lasts for the life of most FHA loans. With conventional private mortgage insurance, you may not need to refinance: you can ask your servicer to cancel it once your balance reaches 80% of the home's original value.

p: Home / Borrower questions / Flood insurance outside a flood zone
Many Gulf Coast homes sit in FEMA's moderate- or low-risk zones. Here is when flood insurance is required, when it's optional, and why timing matters.
Written and reviewed by Brian Lehmann, NMLS #369470, loan officer since 2010 · Updated November 19, 2026 · 4-minute read
Federally backed mortgages require flood insurance only in FEMA's high-risk zones (beginning with A or V), though a lender can require it elsewhere.
Homeowners policies don't cover flooding, including storm surge; flood coverage is a separate NFIP or private policy.
An NFIP policy bought on its own usually takes 30 days to start; one bought as part of a mortgage closing starts at closing.

Homeowners insurance doesn't cover flooding, so many owners near the water buy it anyway, and an NFIP policy bought after closing usually takes 30 days to start.

sections.h: When is flood insurance required for a mortgage?
p: When the home is in a FEMA high-risk flood zone, those beginning with A or V, and the loan is federally backed, which includes most conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA loans. Outside those zones, federal rules don't require it, but your lender may.
Look up the address on FEMA’s Flood Map Service Center before you make an offer. Flood maps change, so check the current map rather than an old listing or survey.
No. Most homeowners policies exclude flood damage, including storm surge and rising water. Flood coverage is a separate policy, from the National Flood Insurance Program or a private insurer.

Wind and rain driven through a damaged roof are usually handled under the homeowners or wind policy. Water that rises from outside is a flood claim. That difference matters on the Gulf Coast, where a hurricane can bring both.
An NFIP policy you buy on your own usually takes 30 days to go into effect. A policy bought as part of closing a mortgage starts at closing instead, so the closing is the easiest time to add it.
Insurers can also stop writing new policies when a named storm threatens, so don’t wait for hurricane season to decide. FloodSmart, FEMA’s consumer site, explains how NFIP policies work.

sections.h: Should I buy flood insurance if it's optional?
p: It depends on the home's elevation, how close it is to the water, and what a quote costs. Get an address-specific quote before you make an offer, even in a moderate- or low-risk zone, and weigh the yearly premium against what you could lose.
The premium also changes your monthly payment if it’s paid through escrow. The Gulf Coast home cost checklist shows how to fold it into your budget.
Often, yes. Lenders accept many private flood policies alongside NFIP policies. Ask your lender before you buy one, and compare the coverage limits and deductibles.
Yes. If a map update puts the home in a zone beginning with A or V and you have a federally backed loan, your servicer will require flood insurance.

When the lender requires it, the premium is usually paid through your escrow account, so it's part of the monthly payment. Optional policies can be paid through escrow or directly, depending on your servicer.

Plenty of buyers want a place at the beach they'll use themselves and rent the rest of the year. Whether it's financed as a second home or an investment property changes the down payment, the rate, and the rules.
Written and reviewed by Brian Lehmann, NMLS #369470, loan officer since 2010 · Updated November 21, 2026 · 4-minute read
A conventional second-home loan allows occasional rentals, but the home can't be run mainly as a rental or be under a management agreement that controls occupancy.

A conventional second-home loan allows occasional rentals, but the home must be yours to use for part of the year, can't be run mainly as a rental, and can't be under an agreement that gives a management company control of who stays there. The rent can't be used to qualify. If the condo will mostly be rented, finance it as an investment property instead.

sections.h: What counts as a second home for a mortgage?
p: Under Fannie Mae's rules, a second home must be suitable for year-round use, used by you for some portion of the year, not primarily used or operated as a rental, not a timeshare, and not subject to an agreement that gives a management firm control over its occupancy.
Second-home loans usually need about 10% down and are priced better than investment-property loans. You tell your lender how you plan to use the home, and that answer has to be true.

sections.h: Can I count the rental income to qualify?
p: Not on a second-home loan. If the lender sees rental income from the property, the loan can still be a second home, but the rent can't be used to qualify. You need to afford the payment on your own income.
If you need the rent to qualify, look at a DSCR or conventional investment loan, which is built for that.

sections.h: What about condo buildings with rental programs?
p: A building with a mandatory rental program, or a management agreement that controls when you can stay, generally doesn't fit a second-home loan. Check the condo's documents and any rental agreement before you make an offer.
Buildings with heavy short-term rental activity can also affect whether the project meets Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines at all. See Gulf Coast condo financing.

sections.h: What changes for taxes and insurance?

In Baldwin County, a second home you don’t rent out can be assessed at 10% of value, like a home you live in, but without the homestead exemption. A rental is assessed at 20%. If you’ll rent the home part of the year, ask the Revenue Commission which class applies. See the Baldwin and Escambia property tax comparison. For lodging taxes, see the Alabama Department of Revenue or the Florida Department of Revenue.

sections.h: How long do I need to be self-employed?
p: Usually two years. Under Fannie Mae's guidelines, less than two years can still work if your most recent personal and business tax returns show a full 12 months of income from the current business, and you earned the same or more before in a field offering the same products or services, or in a job with similar responsibilities.
For conventional loans, Fannie Mae treats you as self-employed if you own 25% or more of the business.

sections.h: What documents will the lender ask for?

sections.h: Do my tax write-offs lower what I can borrow?

sections.h: What if my income dropped last year?

A short note explaining a one-time dip, such as a large equipment purchase or time off for a family reason, helps the underwriter read the numbers.

p: Home / Borrower questions / Manufactured homes on the Gulf Coast
Manufactured homes can be financed with a regular mortgage, but only when the home and land meet a few rules. Near the coast, wind and flood requirements add a few more.
Written and reviewed by Brian Lehmann, NMLS #369470, loan officer since 2010 · Updated November 19, 2026 · 4-minute read
A manufactured home can get a regular mortgage when it sits on a permanent foundation, carries HUD labels, and is titled with the land as real property.
Baldwin and Mobile counties and Escambia County, Florida are in HUD Wind Zone II, so the home must be built for a 100 mph design wind speed.

In Baldwin and Mobile counties and Escambia County, Florida, the home must also be built for HUD Wind Zone II or higher. A home on a leased lot usually needs a different kind of loan.

sections.h: What makes a manufactured home eligible for a mortgage?
p: For a conventional loan, Fannie Mae requires a home built on a permanent chassis, attached to a permanent foundation, with a HUD data plate or certification label for each section, and the home and land legally classified as real property. FHA has similar real property and foundation requirements.

Lenders usually ask for an engineer’s certification that the foundation meets HUD’s permanent foundation guidelines. Homes built under HUD’s federal code carry a HUD certification label on each section; if the labels are missing, ask how to get a replacement before you make an offer.

p: Home / Borrower questions / Buying a condo on the Gulf Coast
With a condo, the lender approves two things: you and the building. Here is how that works in Gulf Shores, Orange Beach, Pensacola, and Perdido Key, and what to check before you make an offer.
Written and reviewed by Brian Lehmann, NMLS #369470, loan officer since 2010 · Updated November 19, 2026 · 7-minute read
A condo loan approves two things: you and the building. The building's budget, reserves, insurance, rentals, and repairs all matter.
Many Gulf Coast beachfront buildings are non-warrantable or not FHA or VA approved, which usually means a specialty loan with more money down.
Condo dues count in your debt-to-income ratio, and in Florida you get the milestone inspection and reserve study before your cancellation window closes.

You qualify for a condo mortgage the same way you would for a house, but the condo building also has to qualify. Conventional, FHA, and VA loans each have project rules covering the association's budget, reserves, insurance, rentals, litigation, and repairs. Many Gulf Coast beachfront buildings don't meet them and need a non-warrantable condo loan, which usually means more money down. Ask your lender to check the building before you make an offer.

sections.h: Can I get a mortgage on a condo?
p: Yes. You qualify with your credit, income, and savings like any other buyer, and the lender also reviews the condo project: the association's budget and reserves, its master insurance policy, how many units are rented or owned by one investor, any lawsuits, and any critical repairs or special assessments.

That second review is why condo loans can surprise people. A buyer can be fully approved and still be unable to use a conventional, FHA, or VA loan on a particular building. Brian checks the project first, so you know which loans fit before you write an offer.

sections.h: What is the difference between a warrantable and a non-warrantable condo?
p: A warrantable condo is in a building that meets Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac project guidelines, so it can get a standard conventional loan. A non-warrantable condo is in a building that doesn't, and it needs a specialty (portfolio or non-QM) loan, which usually means a larger down payment and a higher rate.

Being non-warrantable doesn’t mean a building is a bad buy. It means the loan options are narrower and the costs are higher. The mortgage glossary defines warrantability and the other condo terms you’ll hear.

sections.h: Why do so many beachfront condos fail the lender's review?
p: Usually because of how the building operates, not because of the buyer. The most common reasons on the Gulf Coast are a hotel-style rental program or front desk, a high share of short-term rentals, one owner holding too many units, pending litigation, too little set aside in reserves, and deferred maintenance or critical repairs.

Fannie Mae lists the project types it won’t buy loans in, including condo-hotels and buildings needing critical repairs, and a full review expects the budget to set aside at least 10% for reserves. See ineligible projects and the full review process . The Gulf Coast mortgage guide covers what makes a Gulf Shores condo qualify.

sections.h: Which loan types can I use on a condo?
p: Conventional loans work in warrantable buildings, FHA loans need an FHA-approved project or a single-unit approval, and VA loans need a VA-approved project and a unit you'll live in. Non-warrantable buildings and condos you'll rent out usually call for a portfolio, non-QM, or DSCR investor loan.
Conventional: primary homes, second homes, and investment condos in buildings that meet Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac rules. See conventional loans.
FHA: search HUD’s FHA-approved condo list . In some buildings that aren’t on the list, a single unit can still be approved. See FHA loans.
VA: the building must be on VA’s approved list, and the condo must be your primary residence. See using a VA loan on a Gulf Shores condo.
Rental or vacation condo: a second-home or investment loan, or a DSCR loan qualified on the unit’s rent. See second home vs. investment property.

sections.h: How do HOA dues and condo insurance affect what I can afford?
p: Your monthly condo dues count in your debt-to-income ratio along with the mortgage, taxes, and insurance, so high dues lower the price you qualify for. On the coast, the dues often pay for the building's master policy, including wind, while you buy a separate HO-6 policy for the inside of your unit.

Ask the association what the dues cover, whether flood coverage is on the master policy, and whether any special assessment has been approved or proposed. An approved assessment can add its own monthly bill. The payment calculator on the home page has a field for HOA dues, and the Gulf Coast home cost checklist lists the documents to request.

sections.h: What changed for condo buyers in Florida?
p: Florida now requires condo buildings three or more habitable stories tall to complete milestone structural inspections and a structural integrity reserve study (SIRS). When you buy a resale unit, your contract must say whether those reports apply and have been done, and you get a window to cancel after you receive them.

For Pensacola Beach, Perdido Key, and Navarre condos, read the inspection summary and the reserve study before you’re past the cancellation window. A building that has deferred repairs may raise dues or levy a special assessment to fund them, which changes your payment and can affect whether the building qualifies for financing. See the Florida DBPR guide to milestone inspections and SIRS . Alabama has no matching statewide law, so in Gulf Shores and Orange Beach ask for the reserve study and recent engineering reports directly.

sections.h: What makes mortgage rates change from day to day?
p: Mostly the bond market. Lenders price fixed-rate mortgages off the market for mortgage-backed securities, which tends to move with 10-year Treasury yields. Inflation reports, jobs numbers, and expectations about the Federal Reserve all move those markets, so rates can change several times in one week.

The Federal Reserve doesn’t set mortgage rates directly. Its decisions on short-term rates matter mostly through what they signal about inflation and the economy. That’s why mortgage rates sometimes move before a Fed meeting and barely move on the day itself.

sections.h: What is a rate lock, and when should I lock?
p: A rate lock holds your interest rate and points for a set period, often 30 to 60 days, while your loan is processed. Most buyers lock once they have an accepted offer and a closing date. If rates rise after you lock, your rate stays the same.

Longer locks can cost more, and if your closing slips past the lock date, an extension may carry a fee. Ask whether a float-down option is available if rates fall after you lock. Brian times the lock to your contract and closing date.

sections.h: How can I get a lower rate than the average?

Credit: paying down card balances before you apply can raise your score.
Down payment: on conventional loans, pricing often improves at 20%, 25%, and higher equity levels.
Loan type: VA loans often price below conventional loans for eligible buyers.
Shopping: credit scoring models count multiple mortgage inquiries within a short window, typically 14 to 45 days depending on the model, as a single inquiry.

Estimates only. Your actual rate, APR, and payment depend on credit, loan amount, property, and market conditions.

Property taxes. Alabama taxes a home you live in, or a second home you don’t rent out, on 10% of its appraised value; a rental is taxed on 20%. Florida taxes the full value, and after a sale the assessed value resets toward the price you pay, so budget on the price, not the seller’s bill. See the Baldwin vs. Escambia property tax guide.

Insurance. Homeowners and wind premiums depend on the roof’s age, any FORTIFIED designation, distance to the water, and the hurricane deductible. Near the beach, wind is often a separate policy. Get quotes for the specific home.

Mortgage insurance and fees. Conventional PMI is estimated at 0.6% a year under 20% down; you can ask to cancel it at 80% of the original value, and it ends automatically at 78%. FHA, VA, and USDA fees follow each program’s published schedule.
Pricing a specific home? Walk through the Gulf Coast home cost checklist, or text Brian the address and he’ll check the flood zone, taxes, and roof age with you.
